content: Metal 3D printing can create complex shapes and even combine different materials in a single part, potentially creating components with optimized wear and toughness zones without the need for traditional heat treatment. The argument is that investing in a massive furnace-based facility today might be like investing in steam engine technology on the eve of the diesel revolution. This is a forward-looking critique that Aiguille must take seriously. However, it is important to distinguish between the long-term future and the current commercial reality. As of today, additive manufacturing for large, high-stress components like mining GET is still largely in the R&D phase. The audit of a potential foundry partner, for instance, would assess not just their casting equipment but their sand testing laboratory, their metallurgical analysis capabilities, their pattern-making process, and their quality control records. For a machine shop, the audit would examine the age and accuracy of their CNC machines, their CMM (Coordinate Measuring Machine) inspection capabilities, and the skill level of their machinists. Reliability is assessed by speaking with their existing customers, analyzing their on-time delivery performance, and understanding their production planning and capacity management systems. It can involve co-investing in new technology or tooling. Third, it facilitates collaboration and innovation. Having engineers from Aiguille and a local supplier in the same room, looking at the same part, can solve problems and generate new ideas much faster than endless email chains and video calls across different time zones. Finally, in an era of increasing geopolitical uncertainty and supply chain disruptions (as seen during the COVID-19 pandemic), a robust local supplier network provides a powerful buffer, ensuring continuity of production when global supply chains are in turmoil. A counterargument to the "local first" philosophy is that it can lead to provincialism and a lack of competitiveness. The ideal supply chain for Aiguille would be a blend: a core of reliable local partners for agility and resilience, supplemented by best-in-class global suppliers for materials or technologies that are not available locally. Another objection is that managing a network of smaller, local suppliers can be more complex and time-consuming than dealing with a single, large national or global distributor who can provide a "one-stop shop" service.
